treatment of coal gasiﬁcation wastewater (CGW): Evolution of
dissolved organic matter and biotoxicity

Coal gasiﬁcation wastewater (CGW) contains several types of aromatic pollutants, which impart high biotoxicity
and reduce the quality of anaerobic treatment. Two types of hydrolysis acidiﬁcation processes, namely
microaerobic hybrid reactor (HA-1) and upﬂow anaerobic sludge blanket reactor (HA-2), were developed for
pre-treatment before the anaerobic treatment. The changes in the dissolved organic matter and biotoxicity
were investigated to comprehensively understand the degradation process. The results showed that HA-2
coupled with an anaerobic reactor achieved a 12.3% and 13.4% higher removal efﬁciency for chemical oxygen de-
mand and total phenols, respectively, compared with the coupled process with HA-1. Furthermore, HA-2 could
transform macromolecules into small molecules more efﬁciently and produce fewer intermediates. The coupled
process with HA-2 preferentially removed complex aromatic substances with absorption wavelengths of 285 and
254 nm, according to the sequential orders interpreted from two-dimensional correlation spectroscopy. In addi-
tion, the results of ﬂuorescence excitation-emission-matrix with regional integration analysis revealed that the
contents of typical cyclic compounds in CGW, such as phenolic, heterocyclic, and polycyclic aromatic compounds
were remarkably reduced by HA-2. In addition, HA-2 reduced the toxic unit value of CGW by 67.5% and increased
the resazurin dehydrogenase activity of the sludge by 37.5% during CGW treatment, thus improving the
biotoxicity removal and biodegradability. However, the coupled process with HA-2 did not signiﬁcantly affect
the “indirect estrogenic activity” of CGW. A Pearson correlation analysis indicated that spectral indicators, such
as UV254 and ΦT,n, presented a high positive correlation with the reduction of acute toxicity and organics.

1. Introduction
Coal gasiﬁcation is a clean and efﬁcient energy-conversion method,
and plays an important role in adjusting the energy structure, particu-
larly regarding the situation in China of “rich coal, less oil, lack of gas”
(Shi et al., 2019a). However, a large amount of wastewater is produced
from the coal gasiﬁcation process, containing high concentrations of re-
fractory and toxic compounds, such as phenols, polycyclic aromatic hy-
drocarbons, nitrogen heterocyclic compounds, long chain n-alkanes,
and thiocyanate, among others (Ma et al., 2018a; Zhao and Liu, 2016).
The existence of hazardous compounds in coal gasiﬁcation wastewater
(CGW) constrains industrial development due to its adverse effect on
environmental safety and public health.
In general, CGW is treated successively through the phenol and am-
monia recovery process, biological treatment process, and advanced
treatment process (Ji et al., 2016). Among these, anaerobic treatment
is an indispensable process in which refractory compounds can be de-
graded or converted to easily biodegradable compounds, thus reducing
the toxicity and improving the biodegradability of CGW (Fuchs et al.,
2011; Meckenstock and Mouttaki, 2011; Shi et al., 2019b). However,
for chemical oxygen demand (COD) and total phenols (TPh), a removal
efﬁciency of only 20–30% has been achieved during the anaerobic treat-
ment of CGW with conventional mesophilic upﬂow anaerobic sludge
blanket (UASB) reactors (Wang et al., 2011). The hydrolysis acidiﬁca-
tion (HA) process has been widely used as a pre-treatment process for
various industrial wastewaters (Song et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2014;
Wu et al., 2016) to improve the wastewater-treatment process. In the-
ory, HA can remove toxic compounds, change the composition of refrac-
tory organics, and reduce the concentration of pollutants in CGW, thus
creating suitable conditions for the subsequent anaerobic process (Xu
et al., 2015). However, the role of the HA process has not yet been sufﬁ-
ciently explained.
Moreover, UASB has been extensively used in the anaerobic treat-
ment of various types of wastewater, particularly high-strength indus-
trial wastewaters (Abbasi and Abbasi, 2012; Kong et al., 2019a);
however, its long start-up period, susceptibility to shock loading, and
high amount of suspended solids in the efﬂuents, among others (Kong
et al., 2019b), have motivated the innovation of many processes based
on UASB. For example, anaerobic hybrid reactors, which combine the
sludge bed in the lower zone and bioﬁlm media in the upper zone, per-
form well in industrial wastewater treatment owing to the existence of
both suspended granules and immobilized bioﬁlm (Ramakrishnan and
Surampalli, 2012; Show et al., 2020). In addition, micro-aeration treat-
ment technology has been proved as an effective strategy to improve
the anaerobic process in accelerating hydrolysis, increasing the inhibi-
tion of sulphate reduction, and reducing the massive accumulation of
volatile fatty acids (VFAs), among others (Chen et al., 2020). Further-
more, microaerobic hydrolysis acidiﬁcation has been successfully used
as a pre-treatment process in petrochemical wastewater plants (Wu
et al., 2016). Theoretically, the integration of micro-aeration and the an-
aerobic hybrid process developed in this research can improve the hy-
drolysis of CGW as the pre-treatment for the subsequent biological
treatment.
The transformation of dissolved organic matter (DOM) during the
wastewater treatment process not only reﬂects the removal efﬁciency
of pollutants, but also reveals the reaction mechanism of wastewater
treatment units to some extent, contributing to the selection and opti-
mization of the combined process (Aftab and Hur, 2019; Chen et al.,
2017a; Peng et al., 2018). Recently, spectroscopic methods, such as ﬂuo-
rescence excitation-emission-matrix (EEM) spectroscopy, ultraviolet-
visible (UV–Vis) spectroscopy and Fourier transform infrared spectros-
copy (FTIR), have been widely used to depict shifts in DOM. Further-
more, much more accurate and comprehensive information on the
constituent change of DOM can be acquired with the assistance of pow-
erful mathematical tools, including ﬂuorescence regional integration
(FRI) (Chen et al., 2003), parallel factor analysis (PARAFAC) (Stedmon
and Bro, 2008), and two-dimensional correlation spectroscopy (2D-
COS) (Phong and Hur, 2016). FRI and PARAFAC are EEM quantitative
analysis methods, and 2D-COS method can be employed to reveal the
direction and sequential order of DOM changes. For example, in a previ-
ous study, the degradation behaviour of efﬂuent organic matter in ozon-
ation, UV/H2O2, and UV/persulfate has been revealed by EEM-PARAFAC
and 2D-COS coupled with gel permeation chromatography, and the re-
action mechanism involved in the three advanced oxidation processes
was comprehensively discussed (Chen et al., 2017b). Aftab et al.
(2018) gained novel insights into the DOM oxidation behaviours of
landﬁll leachate in Fenton oxidation processes under different operation
conditions via EEM-PARAFAC and 2D-COS-FTIR. In summary, spectro-
scopic methods coupled with mathematical tools can be used to reveal
the transformation of heterogeneous DOM in CGW, and can therefore
explain the role of the HA process. In addition, some studies have indi-
cated that there exists a correlation between the spectral indicators
and biotoxicity, such as UV254 and the total ﬂuorescence intensity
(Tang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2019), suggesting that spectral indicators
could be used to reveal the complex biotoxicity, hence, will demonstrate
the efﬁciency of wastewater treatment, and the former can be obtained
quickly and cost-effectively. Nevertheless, sufﬁcient information re-
garding spectral indicators and biotoxicity in CGW is not available.
Although several technologies have been applied in CGW treatment
to satisfy the national discharge standard, treated efﬂuent has still been
found to contain some recalcitrant and toxic pollutants, which may pose
a potential risk to ecosystems and human health (Zhu et al., 2018). Var-
ious biotoxicity methods (acute toxicity, genotoxicity, estrogenic activ-
ity, and anti-estrogenic activity) (Ma et al., 2019a) should be used to
obtain comprehensive information on the negative effects of the hetero-
geneous CGW. However, most studies on the biotoxicity of CGW have
focused on the acute toxicity of CGW, and there is a lack of research
for determining the toxic effects based on multi-methods (Ma et al.,
2018b; Xu et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2018). Because the composition of
organic pollutants in CGW through various treatment processes is dif-
ferent, which may cause diverse toxic effects, exploring the evolution
of biotoxicity in CGW anaerobic treatment could directly reveal the de-
toxiﬁcation effects exerted by anaerobes, further providing the critical
reference for the optimization of the anaerobic process and selection
of the subsequent process.
In the present study, two types of HA methods coupled with UASB
were developed for treating CGW. The main objectives of this study
were to: (1) evaluate the efﬁciency of the CGW anaerobic process
with different HA pre-treatments; (2) clarify the role of HA in enhancing
the anaerobic CGW treatment by identifying the transformation of
DOM; (3) explore the variations of the biotoxicity and biodegradability
from inﬂuent to efﬂuent.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Characteristics of wastewater and inoculum
The wastewater used in this research was synthesized with crude
phenol as the carbon source, which was obtained from the coal chemical
industry in Yima, Henan Province. To improve the biodegradability of
the wastewater, approximately 30% (v/v) domestic wastewater was
added. NH4Cl and KH2PO4 were used as the nitrogen and phosphorus
source, respectively. To ensure the normal growth of microorganisms,
mineral salts were added to satisfy the microbial needs for the micro
and trace elements. The ﬁnial concentrations (mg/L) of the mineral
salts in the synthetic wastewater were as follows: CaCl2·2H2O (20),
MgSO4·7H2O (50), FeSO4·7H2O (15), FeCl3·3H2O (1), MnCl2·4H2O
(0.5), ZnCl2 (0.5), CuCl2 (0.5), (NH4)2MoO4·4H2O (0.5), AlCl3 (0.5),
CoCl2·2H2O (0.5), NaBO2·10H2O (0.5), and NiCl2·2H2O (0.5). More-
over, NaHCO3 was added to maintain the pH at 7–7.5. The key character-
istics of the inﬂuent are listed in Table 1.

The inoculated anaerobic granular sludge was acquired from the an-
aerobic treatment unit of a wastewater treatment plant in Harbin
(China). The total suspended solids (TSS) and volatile suspended solids
(VSS) concentrations were 43 g TSS/L and 31 g VSS/L, respectively, and
VSS/TSS was 0.72. One-third of the effective volumes of both the hydro-
lysis acidiﬁcation reactors and the subsequent UASB reactors were inoc-
ulated with the sludge, and the ﬁnal suspended sludge concentrations
were all approximately 10 g VSS/L.
2.2. Experimental design
Two
types
of
hydrolysis
acidiﬁcation
reactors,
namely
a
microaerobic hybrid reactor (HA-1, 600 mm in height, 90 mm in diam-
eter, working volume of 3.5 L) and a UASB reactor (HA-2, 650 mm in
height, 90 mm in diameter, working volume of 3.5 L), were coupled
with two identical UASB reactors (UASB-1 and UASB-2, respectively;
1100 mm in height, 130 mm in diameter, working volume of 14 L) to
treat the synthetic CGW (Fig. S1). The composite ﬁller (150 mm in di-
ameter) used in HA-1 comprises a plastic ring in the middle and some
polyester ﬁbre around it. Five such rings are ﬁxed vertically in HA-1 at
equal intervals at the upper part, occupying approximately 2/3 of the
entire height of the reactor. To economically induce the microaerobic
condition, the top of HA-1 was exposed to air, and the dissolved oxygen
(DO) was maintained at 0.1–0.9 mg/L. The hydraulic retention times of
the HAs and the subsequent UASBs were 12 h and 47 h, respectively.
HA-1 and HA-2 were operated at room temperature, while UASB-1
and UASB-2 were operated at 35 ± 1 °C. All the reactors were fed
from the bottom, and efﬂuent recycling was conducted to maintain
the upﬂow velocity at 0.5 m/h. The biogas of each UASB was collected
using a gas sampling bag, and subsequently, the volume was measured
using a 150-mL syringe.
To reduce the effect of the high toxicity of the inﬂuent, the two sets
of reactors were initially fed with diluted synthetic CGW, and sucrose
was used as an extra carbon source during the acclimation period. The
COD concentration of the inﬂuent was increased step-by-step based
on whether the efﬂuent COD was steady. A comparative investigation
of the performance between HA-1 and HA-2 was conducted at the
steady state, including COD removal, TPh removal, and VFAs and pH
variation. Additionally, the DOM transformation and biotoxicity reduc-
tion along the two sets of reactors were simultaneously determined.
All the aforementioned parameters were measured in triplicate to en-
sure the validity and representativeness of the experimental results.
2.3. Analytical methods
The COD, NH3-N, pH, TSS, and VSS were measured according to the
standard methods (Chinese SEPAC, 2002). The TPh were determined
by bromize-titration (Zhang et al., 2013). The composition of VFAs
was analysed by gas chromatography (GC; GC 7890 N/FID, Agilent,
USA) with ﬂame ionization detection (Wen et al., 2018). The methane
concentration in the biogas was also determined using GC (Agilent
6890A, USA) (Zhang et al., 2018). The composition of organics was
analysed using GC-mass spectrometry (GC–MS) (6890GC-5973/
5975MSD, Agilent, USA).

The

tometer (SHIMADZUUV-2550, Japan). The molecular weight (MW) dis-
tribution of the DOM was measured via high-performance liquid
chromatography with a gel-ﬁltration chromatography (GPC) column;
the calibration curve of the GPC was obtained according to a range of
polystyrene sulfonate standards (Li et al., 2019). Fluorescence EEM
was measured using a ﬂuorescence spectrophotometer (HITACHI F-
7000, Japan). Prior to the EEM measurement, the samples were diluted
to UV254 below 0.05 cm−1 to avoid the inner ﬁlter effect. Furthermore,
some pre-treatment methods were used to remove the Raman scatter
and Rayleigh scattering, to prepare for the FRI analysis (Chen et al.,
2017a).
2.4. Biotoxicity and biodegradability
2.4.1. Acute toxicity test
The acute toxicity was assessed using a bioluminescence inhibition
assay with a Microtox Model 500 analyser (Modern Water Inc., New
Castle, USA). The marine bacterium Vibrio ﬁscheri was used as the test-
ing organism. The basic mode was employed to determine the effective
concentration (EC50) of each sample, which indicated that the biolumi-
nescence of Vibrio ﬁscheri, exposed to the samples, was reduced by 50%
relative to a toxicant-free control. In brief, each sample was diluted to
create four test concentrations, as instructed by the manufacturer, and
Microtox Diluent was used as the toxicant-free control. First, the initial
bioluminescence was measured, and then all the sample diluents were
mixed with the bacterium, and ﬁnally, the bioluminescence was mea-
sured after 15 min to determine the EC50 for each sample. Furthermore,
the toxic unit (TU) was calculated as the reciprocal of the EC50 to reﬂect
the acute toxicity (Na et al., 2017).
2.4.2. Resazurin dehydrogenase activity (DHA)
Dehydrogenase activity is related to the activity of the microbial me-
tabolism in activated sludge. Based on a previous report (Zhu et al.,
2017), the DHA was measured using two types of activated sludge,
one of which was taken from a full-scale municipal wastewater treat-
ment plant, and the other from a bench-scale A/O-MBR for CGW treat-
ment. Brieﬂy, the activated sludge was mixed with samples and a
phosphate buffer solution (PBS) (pH 7.4), and the PBS was regarded
as the control. After 30 min, the DHA of the activated sludge was deter-
mined. In this study, the DHA of municipal sludge (M-S) could indicate
the toxicity of the samples owing to its sensitivity towards CGW, while
the DHA of sludge for CGW treatment (C\\S), already adapted to toxic
pollutants, could characterize the biodegradability of the samples.
2.4.3. Cytotoxicity and speciﬁc toxicity tests
The yeast cells after 4-h exposure to the samples were used to reveal
the cytotoxicity of the samples. The detailed calculation steps can be
found in a previous report (Chen et al., 2017a). Three types of speciﬁc
toxicity were monitored, namely genotoxicity, estrogenic activity, and
anti-estrogenic activity. Genotoxicity was analysed using SOS/umu-
test with Salmonella typhimurium TA1535/pSK1002 (Wang et al., 2007).
As the positive control, 4-Nitroquinoline-Noxide (4-NQO) was applied
to create the dose-response curve for characterizing the genotoxicity
of the samples using the equivalent 4-NQO concentration. Estrogenic
activity was measured using a yeast two-hybrid assay (Nishikawa

2.5. Mathematical analysis
Using the Origin 2016 (OriginLab, USA), multi-peak Gaussian ﬁtting
of the GPC results was performed to calculate the peak areas for a quan-
titative analysis of the variation in the MW. 2D-COS spectra were ob-
tained using the 2D Shige software (Kwansei-Gakuin University,
Japan) based on the UV–Vis data (Phong and Hur, 2016), including a
synchronous and an asynchronous map. The sequential order of the
changes in the UV–Vis spectra could be obtained based on the two gen-
erated spectra; the interpretation procedure is described in detail else-
where (Noda, 2012). EEM-FRI was used to calculate the integrated
volume of the ﬁve ﬂuorescence regions according to a previous method
(Chen et al., 2003). The normalized regional volume and the corre-
sponding percentage of region “i” could be obtained and are expressed
as Φi,n (AU-nm2) and Pi,n (%), respectively; ΦT,n is the sum of each nor-
malized regional volume (Φi,n). The Pearson correlation coefﬁcient was
calculated using the SPSS software (IBM, USA) to analyse the relation-
ship between the spectral indicators and the biotoxicity.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Performance of the two sets of HA-UASB
The basic properties of the inﬂuent and treated efﬂuents during the
steady operation phase are listed in Table 1. As shown in Table 1, HA-2
coupled with UASB-2 (HA-2-UASB) obtained 37.2% and 36.4% removal
efﬁciencies of COD and TPh, respectively, which increased by 12.3%
and 13.4%, respectively, compared to the coupled process with HA-1
(HA-1-UASB). The removal efﬁciencies of COD and TPh in HA-2 were
21.8% and 16.2%, while the corresponding removal efﬁciencies of HA-1
were 12.7% and 15.9%, respectively. HA-2 exhibited a better removal ca-
pacity of COD and TPh, resulting in higher removal of COD and TPh in
the coupled process. The CGW contains many refractory and toxic com-
pounds, inhibiting the activity of microbes. Generally, HA could decom-
pose the complex pollutants and detoxify the wastewater (Song et al.,
2019). The biodegradability of the wastewater was improved after HA,
to ensure that the subsequent UASB would perform better. The TPh con-
tents in the efﬂuents of HA-1 (551.6 ± 13.6) and HA-2 (549.8 ±
14.4 mg/L) were very similar; however, more phenols were removed
in UASB-2 than UASB-1. This might be attributed to the decomposition
of some refractory pollutants, which produced phenols as the
intermediates during anaerobic hydrolysis. In theory, HA-1 should per-
form better than HA-2 with the advantage of more biomass and micro-
aeration stimulation. In contrast, HA-2 enhanced the removal of COD
and TPh compared to HA-1, which might be due to two reasons. On
the one hand, HA-2 obtained a better hydraulic condition, leading to a
higher sludge bed and complete mixing of the sludge and wastewater.
However, in HA-1, the suspended sludge could not mix well with the in-
ﬂuent which was trapped at the bottom by the ﬁller. On the other hand,
more importantly, the long-term exposure of the CGW to oxygen in HA-
1 would result in the generation of some refractory compounds (hetero-
cyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, derivatives of benzene series, etc.) (Zhu
et al., 2018). Although previous reports have indicated that micro-
aeration could effectively promote the diversity and activity of hydro-
lytic and fermentative microorganisms in the AD process (Chen et al.,
2020), the positive effects on the microbes by a small dose of oxygen
seemed to be negligible for high-concentration CGW treatment when
the negative effect of the water quality dominated. More attempts are
required to explore the relation among the DO concentrations, micro-
bial community structure, and CGW components to establish a robust
conclusion of micro-aeration.
UV254 and the speciﬁc UV absorbance (SUVA) are commonly used to
indicate the aromaticity of wastewater. The SUVA of the samples was
determined by dividing UV254 with the DOC concentration. As shown
in Table 1, the removal efﬁciencies of UV254 of HA-1 and HA-2 were
16.9% and 25.2%, respectively; the removal was further enhanced to
23.0% and 28.5%, respectively, by combining HA-1 and HA-2 with the
UASB. Therefore, the UV254 removal during the coupled process de-
pends on the performance of HA. After HA, the SUVA decreased and
then increased in the UASB process. The transformation and degrada-
tion of complex aromatic matters with high aromaticity in the synthetic
CGW caused the decline of the SUVA in the HA. However, only some
small aromatic molecules with lower aromaticity were removed in the
UASB, thus leading to the uptrend of the SUVA (Section 3.2.1).
The VFAs in the inﬂuent and efﬂuent mainly comprised acetates,
while other types of VFAs were negligible (data not shown). The con-
centration of acetates in the efﬂuent of the two HA reactors was approx-
imately 20 mg COD/L, which was lower than that in the inﬂuent.
According to the previous reports, the VFAs concentration could in-
crease if the HA process functioned well (Ma et al., 2019b; Wu et al.,
2015). Thus, the activity of acidifying bacteria was inhibited in both
the HA reactors. Only a slight difference was observed between the ac-
etate concentrations in the efﬂuents of the HA and UASB, indicating that
the activity of methanogens utilizing acetates was also suppressed,
which was in accordance with the methane production in the UASB.
The methane production of the two UASBs ﬂuctuated during the steady
operation period and ranged between 10 and 30 mL/d. The pH of the in-
ﬂuent and efﬂuent was also investigated (Table 1); it remained approx-
imately 7.3 in all the samples, irrespective of the VFA concentrations.

3.2. Transformation of the dissolved organic matter
3.2.1. Change of molecular weight
GPC was used to characterize the MW change of the DOM in the
coupled process. As shown in Fig. 1a, two main peaks were determined
with elution times of 940 s and 1235 s, representing 7654 Da (peak
A) and 107 Da (peak B), respectively. Generally, peak A represents
high-MW organics, like high-MW humic substances; however, the syn-
thetic CGW used in this research mainly comprised aromatic pollutants,
such as phenols and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, but not humic
substances. Considering the intermolecular forces between aromatic
compounds (e.g. hydrogen bonding, π-π interactions, etc.), particularly
for phenols (Vojta and Vazdar, 2014), it was assumed that peak A in this
research represented a mixture of aromatic compounds, connected via
multiple intermolecular forces, which showed the characteristics of
large molecular weight and high aromaticity. Peak B corresponds with
low-MW organics, such as aldehydes, alcohols, and phenols.
To quantify the changes in the MW, multi-peak Gaussian ﬁtting was
used to integrate the peak area using Origin 2016 (Fig. S2). The variation
of the peak area of the samples is shown in Fig. 1b. The major UV254 of
the inﬂuent was sourced from the aromatic mixture (peak A), as
shown in Fig. 1b. After the HA process, the area of peak A decreased
sharply from 51.0 × 104 mV Da to 16.8 × 104 mV Da and
15.9 × 104 mV Da in HA-1 and HA-2, respectively, and then changed
slightly during the UASB process. Meanwhile, the area of peak B initially
increased from 3.2 × 104 mV Da to 25.2 × 104 mV Da and
20.0 × 104 mV Da in HA-1 and HA-2, respectively, and then decreased
to 13.3 × 104 mV Da and 3.5 × 104 mV Da in UASB-1 and UASB-2. It
was evident that the high-MW molecules (peak A) were metabolized
and degraded by microorganisms into relatively low-MW molecules
(peak B) during the HA process. The present result is consistent with
the literature that HA can efﬁciently transform most high-MW DOM
(N100 kDa) in real domestic wastewater into low-MW DOM
(b500 Da) (Liu et al., 2016). Theoretically, for a higher proportion of
low-MW matter, the biodegradability of the wastewater would im-
prove. The good biodegradability of wastewater was closely related to
the fact that small molecules could gain access into bacterial cells
more easily than in high-MW matter (Liu et al., 2016). Therefore, the ef-
ﬂuent of the HA-1 process containing more low-MW matter should be
more suitable for the subsequent anaerobic treatment. However, more
small molecules (peak B) were reduced in UASB-2, although less low-
MW matter (peak B) was present in the efﬂuent of HA-2. A possible rea-
son for this is that the low-MW matter in HA-1 may predominantly
comprise intermediates, such as alcohols, ethers, and ketones, while

3.2.3. Change of ﬂuorescence

as non-destructive for samples. Hence, they have been widely used to
characterize the DOM in both wastewater and natural water systems
(Korak et al., 2014). The EEM ﬂuorescence spectra of all the samples
are presented in Fig. 3. Two evident ﬂuorescence peaks were identiﬁed
from the ﬂuorescence spectra of the inﬂuent. The ﬁrst peak (peak
1) was observed at excitation/emission wavelengths (Ex/Em) of 270/
305 nm; it is related to the π–π conjugated groups of aromatic sub-
stances (e.g. phenols and benzoquinone) (Peng et al., 2018). The second
peak (peak 2) appeared at Ex/Em of 220/300–310 nm, and is associated
with aromatic matter-containing benzene rings (Peng et al., 2018). The
dominant ﬂuorescent peaks indicate that the phenols, benzene, and
their derivates were the primary pollutants in the inﬂuent, which is in
line with previous reports (Zhu et al., 2018).

3.2.4. Identiﬁcation of organic compounds
To conﬁrm the speculation on the transformation and removal of the
DOM in the synthetic CGW along the coupled process, the organic com-
pounds in the inﬂuent and treated efﬂuent were analysed by GC–MS. As
shown in Table 3, the major organic compounds in the inﬂuent and
treated efﬂuent were phenols and their derivatives, accounting for
N50% of the total peak area, while there were few heterocyclic com-
pounds, as well as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, in each sample.
A possible reason for this is that there were only small amounts of het-
erocyclic compounds and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in the
water sample, or that the extraction force of the extractant to those con-
taminants was limited. Furthermore, some kinds of phenols were found
to be totally removed in the coupled process; however, some new con-
taminants were present in the treated efﬂuent (i.e. p-cresol and phenol,
2-ethyl), indicating the transformation of the DOM in the coupled pro-
cess. Such a transformation most probably occurred in the HA process,
based on the analysis of the MW, and UV–Vis and EEM spectra. Simulta-
neously, some ester and long-chain hydrocarbons were generated as in-
termediates in the treated efﬂuent, and more intermediates were
detected in the efﬂuent of UASB-1 compared to that of UASB-2, which
was coincident with the results of the MW distribution analysis, show-
ing that the contaminants were more thoroughly degraded in the
coupled process with HA-2. The spectra and chromatography combined
with advanced mathematic tools could provide further insights into the
DOM transformation in the CGW in the coupled processes.

3.4. Pairwise correlations between regular parameters, spectral indicators
and acute toxicity
The relationships between the regular parameters, spectral indica-
tors, and acute toxicity were determined by the Pearson correlation ma-
trix and are depicted in Fig. 6. The detailed data are listed in Table S2.
The results showed that the regular parameters (i.e. COD, TPh, and
DOC) were positively correlated with each other (R = 0.946–0.974,
P b .05), indicating that the phenolic compounds were the major pollut-
ants in the CGW. Meanwhile, the COD was positively associated with
UV254, ΦI,n, ΦIV,n, ΦT,n, and TU (R = 0.882–0.974, P b .05), and TPh was
positively related to these parameters, except ΦT,n and TU (P N .05), in-
dicating that the CGW comprised various aromatic compounds besides
phenols, and that the reduction of the acute toxicity was attributed to
the removal of all the organics in the CGW, not limited to the phenols
removal. Furthermore, it was found that UV254, the chromatogram
area of ﬁtted peak A (GPC-A), ΦI,n, ΦII,n, ΦIV,n, and ΦT,n were positively
correlated (R = 0.939–1.000, P b .05), suggesting the unsaturated mat-
ters in CGW were related to aromatic pollutants, and the hypothesis
that GPC-A was the assemblage of various aromatic substances based
on multiple intermolecular forces could be proved to some degree. In
addition, it is worth noting that the TU had a strong and positive corre-
lation with UV254, GPC-A, ΦI,n, ΦII,n, ΦIV,n, and ΦT,n (R = 0.976–0.993,
P b .01), and the highest relationship appeared between ΦT,n and TU,
implying that the acute toxicity was mainly caused by the aromatic mat-
ters in the CGW. Therefore, it was clear that the variation of the regular
parameters and acute toxicity during the anaerobic treatment of the
CGW could be adequately depicted by the spectral indicators, particu-
larly UV254 and ΦT,n.
4. Conclusion
HA played a key role in the DOM transformation, wastewater detoxi-
ﬁcation, and biodegradability improvement. Compared to HA-1, HA-2-
UASB achieved a better performance regarding the removal of organic
pollutants. Moreover, HA-2 had an advantage over HA-1 in transforming
the DOM, which was mainly reﬂected in three aspects: (1) HA-2 con-
verted more macromolecules into small molecules with less intermedi-
ates; (2) with the help of HA-2, the coupled process preferentially
removed complex aromatic substances with absorption wavelengths of
285 and 254 nm; (3) HA-2 achieved a higher removal of typical cyclic
compounds, including refractory aromatic substances. Furthermore, a
dramatic reduction in the acute toxicity and improvement of the biode-
gradability was obtained in HA-2. Meanwhile, the “indirect estrogenic ac-
tivity” in the CGW should cause concern for researchers. A Pearson
correlation analysis revealed that spectral indicators could be alternatives
for revealing the variation in the regular parameters (i.e. COD and TPh)
and the acute toxicity during the anaerobic treatment process of CGW,
and a signiﬁcant correlation was observed between the aromatic com-
pounds and acute toxicity. This study demonstrated that spectral indica-
tors showed high potential in monitoring the performance of practical
CGW treatment.
